Mr. Speaker, to be consistent, I must support this amendment as well. The art of being a good parliamentarian lies in one's being willing to compromise. It is refreshing to hear a Liberal espousing something that sounds like the concept of free trade. The last time I remember free trade being espoused was in the Dunning budget, almost two generations ago. I believe that anybody, in any corner of this House, who supports free trade will have little difficulty in finding support in Western Canada. Western Canada has only gone ahead twice. The first time was under a Liberal administration, led by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, when the matter of reciprocity with the United States was discussed. After that, western Canada went ahead on sporadic occasions when this country sought free trade in the markets of the world.
I should like to see more free trade, because I have seen what it can mean. At this time Chemcell has thought it necessary to lay off between 325 and 350 breadwinners in my constituency. The firm is keeping open that part of its factory that is producing textiles. I think we ought to look more closely at this. A third of the factory is busy producing textiles from petrochemicals and artificial fibres. If we cannot compete, in areas like the production of so-called Irish linen made in Red China, then perhaps we could concentrate on making materials in which we have the upper hand, materials made from cheap petrochemicals. I conclude in this category wood products. It is in these areas that an alert government of a progressive nation such as Canada could make headway, and it is here that we could bring about the rationalization of which the minister spoke eloquently when introducing this bill. I certainly support free trade, and I say without hesitation that I would support any group in Canada which espoused the concept of free trade. I believe that free trade and free enterprise is the only basis on which we can have a free world.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jerry Pringle (Fraser Valley Easi) moved:
subtopic: CUSTOMS ACT
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR PROVISION OF QUALIFIED PERSONNEL AT AIRPORTS TO FACILITATE CLEARANCE OF AIRPLANE TOURIST TRAFFIC
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of making regulations, pursuant to paragraph (r) of section 273 of the Customs Act, so as to facilitate airplane tourist traffic at Canadian airports of entry by providing for the deputizing of qualified personnel now employed at management or administrative officers to handle customs clearance of such tourist traffic.
He said: Mr. Speaker, about a year ago I was privileged to present this resolution to the House. Although no opposition was forthcoming during the hour devoted to private members' bills, no direct action was taken to get Parliamentary approval. During the past year I have met with representative groups within the general aviation industry. On several occasions I have been encouraged by them to resubmit my resolution and continue the debate.
At page 897 of Hansard for November 17, 1969, my speech is recorded in which I endeavoured to explain the problems of general aviation as related to customs clearance for aircraft tourist traffic at ports of entry in Canada. I do not propose to repeat the explanation today. I am sure that most hon. members are familiar with the problems. I know that many members have received letters from aviation enthusiasts, businessmen and associations with regard to the problem relating to customs clearance for tourist traffic at airports.
I will attempt to suggest evidence which will hopefully provide the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gray) with sufficient proof to influence a new and realistic approach to this subject. However, I feel it is incumbent upon me to reiterate my remarks pertaining to the confidence of the travelling public in our customs and immigrations officials, especially their conduct in handling airplane tourist traffic. I suggest no criticism with regard to these officials in the performance of their duty.
Airports of entry differ from automobile ports because they are not located at the exact point of entry into Canada. Airports accommodating international passenger and commercial traffic are properly designated to serve the travelling public and in many instances are located two to three hundreds miles north of the Canada-USA border. Full time customs and immigration officers and offices are, of course, permanently located at international airports regardless of location. Light plane traffic is still permitted to use international airports of entry, and in fact, under existing regulations are encouraged to take advantage of this round-the-clock service, even though there is some doubt as to the advisability of mixing fast jet traffic with the slower light planes.
This resolution is designed to lend assistance and expedite customs clearance for light plane tourist traffic at smaller airports of entry located close to the border. Most
Customs Act
of the smaller airports of entry are no longer provided with service beyond regular working hours, as well as weekends and holidays. I would like to qualify that statement inasmuch as some still have adequate service, but most are denied the service which allows for the convenience of the tourist traffic using aircraft. The system automatically causes inconvenience to customs officers as well as airplane operators.
I am pleased to extend the appreciation of dozens of pilots I have talked to, as well as organizations which have only compliments to hand out as far as courteous treatment is concerned. I'm sure the time involved in travelling to and from these smaller airports of entry create time consuming inconveniences to customs officers, especially where an office is staffed by one officer.
A study of the recent re-organization of district and area administrations indicates the Department of National Revenue and the Department of Immigration have improved the efficiency of service to Canadian communities without adding cost to the tax-payers. The temporary employment of university students during peak traffic periods during the summer is highly commendable and I am sure is appreciated by both the tourists and the students. Each year community airports are being improved and light plane traffic is gradually increasing. More and more people are taking advantage of the convenience provided by new sophisticated equipment found in modern light airplanes and small airports. They are able to avoid the congested highway traffic and get above the polluted air into the blue sky.
In Canada today there are more than 10,000 registered aircraft. Light aircraft account for all but a few hundred, and I include airline transports in this figure. I repeat, of the 10,000 aircraft, and I am referring to all aircraft apart from the military, light aircraft accounts for all but a few hundred. Our real tourist potential is most impressive. There are 700,000 licensed pilots in the United States. Out of 130,000 registered airplanes in the United States, 98 per cent are owned by non-airline people. The Federal Aviation Administration in the U.S. estimates that 50 per cent of all air passengers in the United States are carried by non-airlines aircraft. Therefore, flying tourist traffic offers great potential, but lack of customs clearance assurance at many Canadian ports of entry discourages our American friends from travelling to Canada in light aircraft.
The concept that only the idle rich can afford private airplanes is no longer valid. Canadians and Americans in all walks of life are registered owners and pilots. Literally thousands of farmers on both sides of the border utilize various types of aircraft to facilitate emergency trips to centres for repair parts, fence inspections, aids to round up of cattle, crop spraying and so on. The farmers like to be tourists as well. However, most airports are located some distance from our urban centres, hence the general public is unaware of the ever increasing light plane traffic. I suggest that those who are interested should visit their local airport, especially on the weekend when there is not convenient customs clearance, and count the number of airplanes. In fact, light plane traffic

March 22, 1971
Customs Act
has been increasing so rapidly during the past few years that governments, in their wisdom, have been endeavouring to entice light airplane traffic away from major international airports in the interests of easing congestion. Governments have also been increasing aid for development of smaller airports in both rural and urban areas. Light plane pilots appreciate the concern of the Ministry of Transport and are happy to co-operate by utilizing airports outside the busy traffic patterns and corridors used by high flying, pressurized transports.
The resolution under debate at the present time has been criticized on the grounds that responsible airport managers or assistants would have difficulty in mastering the techniques relating to the duties of customs officers as established by existing criteria. It has been suggested that a conflict of interest might exist by virtue of the desire of airport managers to place priority on service to the travelling air tourists above the responsibilities of customs officers. This argument might have possessed some validity in days gone by when the gas boy operated the airport. Only in a very few isolated cases does it apply today. The airports which might qualify under the terms of reference of this resolution are usually owned outright by municipalities and operated by duly appointed airport boards under the able management of responsible citizens. Airport managers and their assistants for the most part are charged nowadays with the responsibility of administering strict rules as prescribed by the airport board and air regulations. Private operators handle gas concessions and engineering services.
I do not suggest, Mr. Speaker, that all existing small airports of entry in Canada would qualify. I am sure there are probably a sizeable number which would not expect to qualify under this resolution. But I do say there are many airports of entry which could and should qualify if the Minister of National Revenue were to establish criteria based on a fair approach to the situation. I am not sufficiently presumptuous to attempt to set forth essential requirements but perhaps I might make a few suggestions for consideration.
First, the effect of this resolution, if it is adopted, might apply only to airports of entry within reasonable proximity of existing customs offices. Second, applicants would be required to enter upon a period of training acceptable to the Department of National Revenue. Third, tourist traffic only would be handled by the deputized officers, and this would be done in the same way as students handle seasonal duties. There is considerable experience in this regard. Many commercial flights today cannot be handled at airports of entry and customs officers must make special arrangements for commercial entries. If there is dutiable merchandise of a kind not ordinarily carried by tourists, it must be taken to the downtown customs office, and so on. Thus, the separation of tourists from commercial traffic is not entirely new. Fourth, deputized officers would be responsible to local customs officers and would be called upon to provide essential reports on a regular basis as required. Finally, a
small user charge would be imposed in order to eliminate any cost to the taxpayers as a whole.
You might feel, Mr. Speaker, that this is a generous statement to make on behalf of the various airport operators of Canada, but I can assure you there is a great need for traffic development at these airports in which municipalities, the business community and the flyers themselves have invested heavily to assist in the growth of the aviation pattern. I am confident that if criteria were established, together with a small user charge prescribed by the Minister of National Revenue, the airport managers and those who qualify to become deputized officers would be happy to co-operate in levying the charge; they would be glad to operate within the budget which might be made available, without cost to the taxpayer.
The greatest concern of the flying public centres on the fact that at many airports of entry after 5 p.m. on weekdays, all day Saturdays, Sundays and holidays, no service exists. This is unrealistic. Tourist traffic reaches its peak between Friday afternoon and Sunday evening. Service at weekends and after 5 p.m. is available at most airports of tourist destination only on payment of heavy travelling fees, anywhere from $12 to $30. The time taken to clear an airplane arriving with tourists is about 10 or 15 minutes.
In closing, I plead with the House to permit the referral of my resolution to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications. I respectfully suggest that the proposition is practicable and worthy of further consideration. If the Minister of National Revenue, after committee hearings, could establish a pilot project I am sure the aviation industry would be grateful and only too happy to render all possible assistance to the department as well as to the customs collection officers, so that we could eliminate the serious problem to which I have referred, one which is confronting general aviation today when people are travelling in Canada as tourists.

subtopic: CUSTOMS ACT
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR PROVISION OF QUALIFIED PERSONNEL AT AIRPORTS TO FACILITATE CLEARANCE OF AIRPLANE TOURIST TRAFFIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have no hesitation in rising to support the ideal behind this motion. I have not had the opportunity to travel extensively by private aircraft but the complaints the hon. member has mentioned have been forcibly brought to my attention over the years by the operator of a small boat in a border area of southwestern Ontario. Getting properly passed through customs often poses a considerable problem, particularly at weekends when customs offices are open short hours at ports of entry which are operated on a seasonal basis.
As far as the customs officers themselves are concerned, may I go on record as stating that in most instances they are most co-operative. With plans properly made out in advance, customs inspection should not normally present any serious difficulty. I am more concerned about the situation where a large group of passengers arrive at one of our airports and some 100 or so people are subjected to delays that in this type of operation are literally abominable. These passengers do not know where their baggage is and they have to stand around waiting. This is where consternation reigns supreme.

March 22, 1971

An honest appraisal of the situation would lead almost anybody to the conclusion that these delays are definitely not caused by customs or immigration officials but, in my humble opinion, are caused by the administration and operation of the airport itself. Eventually, people's bags are found, though sometimes a report comes through that the bags of people who are in Ottawa are on their way to Winnipeg. However, my point is that delays at airports are primarily not the fault of customs inspectors.
I suggest that some streamlining of procedures, as is the case in other jurisdictions, could be made to assist the situation. For example, travellers could be placed on their honour to exit through one door if they have nothing to declare and to go another way if they do have something to declare. This procedure would be much better, it seems to me, than deputizing management or administrative officers, particularly at large airports, having full regard to the suggestions the hon. member made in connection with smaller airports.
For example, what management would be deputized at a large international airport? The manager of the cafeteria, the manager of the bar, the administrative officers, or whom? If these people cannot do a better job of effecting entry of tourists into this country than they do of sorting baggage, then I suggest that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gray), who is in the House, better stick to the tried and true method of the trained and qualified customs examiners. I am all in favour of speeding up procedures adopted by administrative officers at our large airports, since they have not set any records in the handling of my luggage, but I submit that most customs officers are pretty efficient and surely their specialized training is worth something in this instance.

subtopic: CUSTOMS ACT
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR PROVISION OF QUALIFIED PERSONNEL AT AIRPORTS TO FACILITATE CLEARANCE OF AIRPLANE TOURIST TRAFFIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to support the notice of motion before the House, may I say I have great pleasure in suggesting that such a term of reference for the Standing Committee on Transport and communications would make for good debate. The hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Pringle) could elaborate on his motion in committee to a greater extent than he has been able to do in the House. However, I believe there is good reason for supporting the notice of motion in view of certain things that need attention, and of which I am sure the hon. member is aware. Regardless of how much we would like to believe that there is sufficient staff available at all times to effect speedy customs clearance, the fact remains that there are occasions when deputies are required. In this regard, one of the areas that bears considerable examination, in my humble opinion, is the method of handling the jumbo jets. Since we are just about to enter the jumbo jet age, I feel we should have some extra facilities and manpower to handle the increased number of passengers carried by these aircraft.
I was concerned the other day to discover that Air Canada is considering discontinuing two of its normal flights to Vancouver when the jumbo jets are introduced so that these large aircraft will be filled. To me this is a further indication that the arrival of a jumbo jet will require extra personnel to handle customs clearance, lug-
Customs Act
gage, and passengers generally. At the present time we have a fairly efficient system of handling passengers at our airports. Yet we are bringing in the jumbo jet service without giving any consideration at all to the way we will handle their cargoes.
Further, it strikes me that the first image a tourist or visitor to Canada gets of this country is in the way he is treated at the port of entry. Unless we have sufficient facilities to cope with these visitors and to greet them properly, I am afraid our image is going to suffer.
I think the notice of motion introduced by the hon. member for Fraser Valley East at least opens the door to further consideration of this question in committee. Perhaps the government will think of other ways to handle the problem at that time, but surely at the present time we should allow this notice of motion to go forward to committee for discussion with a view to effecting speedy customs clearance. Even though there may be reservations about the mechanics of the notice of motion, we have no hesitation in giving our support to sending the motion forward to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: CUSTOMS ACT
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR PROVISION OF QUALIFIED PERSONNEL AT AIRPORTS TO FACILITATE CLEARANCE OF AIRPLANE TOURIST TRAFFIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by commending the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Pringle) for his initiative in putting forward for consideration the important matter raised in his notice of motion. I think I can say that this action on his part is typical of his continuing efforts as an effective and constructive member, not only on behalf of his constituents but also with respect to matters of public interest in general. I think I can inform the House that prior to the presentation of his motion today I arranged for the hon. member to discuss the proposal with senior officials of the customs and excise division as a way of aiding its meaningful consideration.
With reference to the remarks made by the last two speakers, I would certainly be pleased to hear from hon. members with regard to any problems they feel exist in relation to customs service in their areas so that I can have them looked into. Also, while the motion itself does not pertain directly to the matter of handling passengers from jumbo jets, I think I can say that planning to provide adequate customs service on arrival of jumbo jets has been carried out with the aim of ensuring that this kind of service is in fact available. I have been pleased to hear the compliments extended by hon. members to customs officers for the manner in which they have carried out their duties.
Let me now make a few comments on the subject matter of the motion itself. As some hon. members are probably aware, for many years prior to 1968 customs service for the clearance of non-commercial tourist air traffic in Canada was provided at all times without charge. The only cost to the parties accommodated was the payment of any transportation expense which departmental officers might incur in providing the service. Before 1968, call-out customs service was provided to

March 22, 1971
Customs Act
what are known as health or pleasure flights arriving at any airport approved for customs entry. This meant that customs officers were on call during the hours of operation of these airports. Since service to these flights was not subject to special service charges, the Customs and Excise Division was obliged to compensate officers with overtime pay for providing clearances after their regular hours of duty.
I should like to point out, however, that current regulations do not permit the charging of special services other than for the transportation of an officer when pleasure craft clearances are involved. This meant that before 1968 a situation existed in respect of service at small tourist airports whereby operators were receiving service which far exceeded that accorded any other form of transportation and that the cost of providing such service was being absorbed by the taxpaying public generally. I think I can best illustrate the point by referring to the facilities available at certain highway offices on the Canada-U.S.A. border where service is provided during specific hours and persons wishing to enter Canada outside those hours must do so at points of entry where extended or 24-hour service is available, and this has been the case for some time.
During 1968 it was recognized that the financial obligations of the government under contract with its employee groups about pay for call-out duties had become quite significant. It was considered that if this trend was continued as a result of future negotiations, costs in providing after-hours service to tourist air traffic would be completely out of proportion to the cost of service rendered to the travelling public as a whole. In view of this, and because of the budgetary and manpower restrictions placed on government operations at that time, it became necessary to review this function to ensure effective operation within the budgetary means available to the department.
Therefore, a revised policy governing hours of service at customs airports for the clearance of pleasure aircraft was put in effect in the late summer of 1969. Under this new system certain airports were designated, in network fashion, throughout all regions of Canada at which aircraft arriving with destinations in Canada could report inward for customs purposes. All other small airports would be confined to regular port hours, Monday through Friday. The aim was to encourage operators of aircraft to make their after-hours clearances at the specially designated airports I mentioned.
Generally speaking, after-hours service continued to be available for any air traffic entering Canada in need of it, although not always at each individual landing strip or airfield in the country. It was realized that this network approach would not be completely acceptable to pleasure air traffic in all instances and that we could still expect requests for clearances at other hours at certain airports. Such additional call-out service could, under present regulations, only be provided on an advance notice basis and then, in effect, at the expense of the taxpayer at large.
As one can well appreciate, the necessary curtailment of hours at certain airports, which over the years had given unlimited service, has given rise to a series of representations by individuals and organizations as well as in the form of this private member's motion calling for legislation authorizing the appointment of persons other than regular customs officers to perform the customs duties after regular hours at small airports. While the motion has been given a lot of thought and in-depth study, I regret that it is not felt this proposal can be accepted, at least in its present form.
I am advised that the only existing exception to the present situation with regard to use of regular customs officers is in respect of certain remote locations in the Arctic where Royal Canadian Mounted Police officers are normally used as customs officers or, when none are available, other government officials are used. But I am informed that ordinary civilians are never used for the position of part-time or temporary officer in the Arctic area. So, as I have said, I think it could be argued that the hon. member's motion, at least in the form in which it has been presented today, is not acceptable for a number of reasons. Let me list some of these reasons for the consideration of the House. The department, in order to demand proper service, of course would be obliged to adequately compensate such persons for performing the additional duties, and this would likely be on the same basis as payment to regular officers for such service. However, it is felt the service provided would not likely be up to the standard required by the law the department administers, and departmental requirements.
Another point is that it could well be that questions might be raised concerning how the proposal would fit into the collective bargaining arrangements between the government and its employees. Also, it should not be overlooked that customs officers assigned to the clearance of aircraft are responsible not only for the administration and enforcement of customs laws and regulations but must also act on behalf of many other departments, such as Manpower and Immigration, National Health and Welfare, Agriculture and the Air Transport Committee, to name just a few. I have some doubt that my colleagues who head these other departments or are responsible for some of the other agencies concerned would want to have what essentially would be untrained and part-time personnel to carry out the duties required by these departments and agencies. I think the consent of these departments and agencies would be necessary in respect of any changes along the lines proposed by the hon. member. Of course, as I have suggested, persons outside the customs service certainly could not be expected to perform the work of the customs officers or work on behalf of the other departments concerned without appropriate periods of training.
With specific reference to the hon. member's proposal for the employment of airport management or administrative personnel as part-time customs officers, situations could arise where the airport attendant would be endeavouring to sell his services to the aircraft operator and, on the other hand, causing the operator to present

March 22, 1971

himself, his aircraft and baggage for inspection. He would be called upon to question the operator relative to compliance with immigration regulations, to collect duties and taxes which may be applicable, and possibly would be required to initiate seizure action because of violations detected. I think it could be argued that such an arrangement could result in a conflict of interest on the part of the deputized individual.
Also, one could ask whether the general public would have sufficient respect for someone who was not truly a departmental officer. I say all this recognizing full well the positive development of local and municipal airports and the development of their staffs in recent years. I should say that as a result of the consideration of representations from the hon. member and others I have instructed senior officials of the department to re-examine and re-assess the whole subject of customs services to the travelling and importing public after normal hours at smaller airports throughout Canada. A very comprehensive study is being carried out covering the entire country from coast to coast and in the north.
At the moment, of a total of 138 airports, 67 or almost half are provided with customs service on an extended basis. That is to say, the services given are beyond the normal 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday business hours and vary according to the volume of traffic from 24 hours a day, seven days a week, down to the provision of service from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. Monday to Thursday and 8 a.m. to midnight Friday to Sunday. An example of the latter is the airport at Regina. The remaining half of the total airports are provided with service from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday to Friday with a few receiving slightly longer hours of service.
One-third of all customs airports are located at or near the Canada-U.S.A. border and give extended service to the public, while another third are too far inland to be reached by most pleasure aircraft. Aircraft, therefore, must also pass a number of airports providing adequate service en route to their destination in the remote areas. The balance of our ports are in the limited service category where requests for extended service cannot be justified under any circumstances.
The hon. member had previously suggested to me directly that more extended service is necessary at eight airports, namely, Goderich, Ontario, St. Jean, Quebec, Fredericton, New Brunswick, Moncton, New Brunswick, Digby, Nova Scotia, Weyburn, Saskatchewan, Pitt Meadows, British Columbia and Chilliwack, British Columbia. As a result, I asked that a study be made by the department of the total need for customs service at these and other airports throughout the various regions of Canada. With respect to the eight airports in question, the study to date appears to reveal that of these airports only Fredericton would be likely to qualify for additional service. The Fredericton situation is presently being looked into with a view to seeing exactly what changes could be made to provide more flexible service there.
Also, an extension of service in this way through greater flexibility has recently been put into effect in the
Customs Act
Prairie region of Canada. It was recognized that existing circumstances differ somewhat from those in other regions in that the distance to be travelled can be quite significant, and also there was recognition of the fact that the Prairies had relatively few places where extended hours of service were available. This is similar to steps recently taken with regard to the Kitchener-Waterloo airport after it became apparent that the need for a form of extended service existed.
Accordingly, I recently met with representatives of the airport commission to discuss this matter after receiving representations from various members, particularly the hon. member for Kitchener (Mr. Hymmen). Pending completion of the comprehensive study I have mentioned earlier, a study which involves further discussions with other government departments concerned, I have asked Customs and Excise officials to interpret and apply the existing regulations with respect to service after normal hours at the Waterloo-Wellington airport and other similar smaller airports in the most flexible possible manner in order to accommodate the needs of the travelling and importing public who use such airports.
In conclusion, may I say that subject to the results that might arise from the further consultation and the studies now under way that I have just mentioned, the evidence presently available to the department does not indicate a clear need for additional designations of customs airports with extended hours of service. Also, the question of authorizing private and municipal airport personnel as special, part-time customs agents appears to present a number of practical difficulties, some of which I have outlined and which I think can well lead to the conclusion that the hon. member's proposal, at least in the form he has presented it-although the aims of the hon. member are understood and appreciated-cannot presently be accepted.
Let me assure the House and the hon. member that if our continuing studies lead to the conclusion that additional service is required, then the Customs and Excise division will certainly attempt, consistent with the resources available to it, to provide such service. I wish again to assure the hon. member that the important issue raised in his motion is under active study and I commend him for his initiative in presenting his motion, a step which assists us in the consideration being given to the important question raised by it.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to take part briefly in this debate and to support the hon. member's motion. In my remarks I wish to broaden the subject somewhat. Perhaps you will not rule me out of order, Mr. Speaker, if I discuss the clearing of tourists and visitors to Canada through customs and extend it to those people who arrive by boat, by yacht and by pleasure craft in the Great Lakes area. I shall only take a minute.
Since the minister is in a mood to hear representations and maintain an open mind on the subject, I would ask him to give very serious consideration to a representation that has already been made to his department by letter. This matter concerns clearing of pleasure craft on the
4488

March 22, 1971
Customs Act
north shore of Lake Erie, particularly in Long Point Bay and the inner bay: The particular spot is Booth's Harbour. The Customs Department last year saw fit to extend, on a seasonal basis, a clearing station at this local marina where, by the way, very extensive facilities are being provided and extended to take care of American tourists.
The minister's department knows full well that this is an expanding business on the Great Lakes. The extension of the service on a seasonal basis last year was much appreciated. I understand it was done on a trial basis. This year the local marina at Booth's Harbour has been advised that the service is being withdrawn after only one year. Since the service and the marina are, as I have stated, in the process of expansion, I think it is only fair that the department should take another look at this service and give it at least a two-year trial to determine whether or not it is worth while, because this manner of visiting Canada is being used increasingly by pleasure craft through Lake Erie.
While I am on this subject I would like to express my personal gratitude for the way in which the minister's department a number of years ago handled a rather unpleasant incident in Port Dover, where U.S. visitors were given rather shabby treatment when they attempted to obtain customs clearance. This problem has been cleared up to the satisfaction of the community. I trust the minister will give the same consideration to the representation I now make to him, which I have already placed on paper by means of a letter to his department with respect to seasonal service in Booth's Harbour. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for letting me broaden the topic and make this representation to the minister.

speakeroldname: Mr. Martin P. O'Connell (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
subtopic: CUSTOMS ACT
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR PROVISION OF QUALIFIED PERSONNEL AT AIRPORTS TO FACILITATE CLEARANCE OF AIRPLANE TOURIST TRAFFIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no one can listen except with sympathy to the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Pringle) when he puts a case as cogently as he did here this afternoon. I was very happy therefore to hear the minister responding in a sympathetic way as indeed I feel he has impressed all of us in the House with the strength of the case he made for improved customs services for aircraft for tourism purposes.
However, and in spite of the fact that I think our feeling of sympathy is increased by knowledge of the member's own experience, flying not only for pleasure but for business, and in spite of the fact that most of us appreciate that general aviation in Canada has been neglected in the basic services it requires in favour of interest in very large hub airports, like the international airports and major airports in other cities, I think the case he is making really has to be made elsewhere than to the minister responsible for customs and excise.
To me, a very important consideration is a national airport system that will put the case for general aircraft facilities and service into perspective, so that this traffic will increase in keeping with improved ground and operational facilities and will so increase that the pressure on

the customs people will be great enough to justify the additional expense of providing customs officers as suggested by the hon. member for Fraser Valley East (Mr. Pringle). 1 make this comment in light of some of the statistics which are available. I would like to refer particularly to a recent report of the Central Ontario Aviation Council which draws attention to this neglect of general aviation facilities, including those for tourist aircraft. For example, it points out that in North America there are some 3,000 commercial airliners, but they compete for airport space and indeed for air space with 154,000 general aviation aircraft. Among the latter are aircraft flying for pleasure. That is to say, there is a 50 to 1 proportion in which general aviation aircraft have a preponderance over the major airliners, and it is expected that by the end of this decade that proportion will be more in the order of 100 to one in favour of general aviation aircraft. Therefore, I suggest that the problem which the hon. member has put so cogently in front of us is going to intensify and that this will require the federal government-I think in this case, in collaboration with other governments in Canada-to come up with a national air transportation policy.
Such a policy should include the development of regional, subregional and area airports, not only to cope with this impending traffic but also to encourage its expansion for the economic benefits which it is bound to bring. So I suggest to the hon. member that I think the problem, which is going to intensify, will bring its own solution in its train-that is to say, the build-up in traffic will tend to justify the customs costs which the minister has indicated at present would not be justified.
The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gray) outlined very clearly the changes and improvements that have been made in the customs service to date. I took note of some of them as he went along. I was encouraged, as I am sure the hon. member for Fraser Valley East was, to note that there have been specific improvements along the line of his hopes since 1968. These included changes that brought increased customs services to a certain number of airports where they could be justified. They included changes that made emergency landings open to customs services without additional charges, and a very broad interpretation of emergency services was given. However, I think the problems which the minister mentioned are very formidable, particularly with respect to the solution that the hon. member for Fraser Valley East was putting forward, and for this reason I cannot support the specific proposals of the hon. member in this motion.
In addition to the problems of costs, I do not see how one can get around the problem of deputizing important customs functions to non-customs officers and, in fact, to civilians. Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but customs officers are also obliged to act on behalf of other departments of government when performing their duties, for example, for the Department of Manpower and Immigration, for the Department of National Health and Welfare and also for other departments.
So, Mr. Speaker, in addition to the high cost of supplying after-hours customs services, it seems to me that the hon. member's proposal meets these other formidable
March 22, 1971

objections. It would be a downgrading of customs services. It would be offering a service that really is not adequate in a responsible sense. I suggest that the best solution is likely to be found by pursuing the present course, which is a continually close examination of the situation across Canada, adding after-hours customs services where and when they appear to be justified.
I suggest, therefore, to the hon. member that he should seek other proposals to put forward, because obviously the minister is looking at the matter very sympathetically. I wonder if a bonding system would make sense, so that a pleasure aircraft arriving for tourist purposes might be bonded at a regional airport and then be able to land at a more distant and isolated one where the officials at the airport, not being customs official at the time of landing, might be able to cope with the situation. I am sure that the hon. member, resourceful as he is, will come forward with other proposals that do not raise such formidable objections as have been raised to this current proposal.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, an interesting bill is before us and I hope my few words will be acceptable to the House. I think the bill embodies two propositions and I will put them into my own brand of English. One is: Don't put people in jail; putting people behind bars is a Canadian habit we should all try to discourage. My second colloquial proposition is: Just because they're broke doesn't mean they are criminals; or, people can be poor and honest. That is my way of looking at it. The minister put it in somewhat more refined English in the press release or communique which invariably comes out when a bill is read the first time in the House, dated January 22, 1971. He put it this way:
The basic philosophy of the bill is that a police officer should not arrest a suspect if the public interest can be secured by proceeding otherwise; and that if a suspect is arrested and detained, his financial means should not be the determining factor in deciding whether or not he is released on bail pending his trial. The bill provides that the onus should be on the authorities to establish why bail should not be granted.
Perhaps because of that last statement several police officers' associations expressed concern to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. Their point was graphically made by a cartoon which appeared in an American publication. It depicts an American police officer standing in front of his desk sergeant. The police officer is saying, "I just made an arrest and I would like to call my lawyer."
Some of us are aware of the difficulties that police officers have encountered in an age where some rather important changes have been made to the law. I think I speak for members of the committee when I say that despite the protestations of police associations and some very distinguished police officers, they did not really make their case. However, because they were concerned about it, it would be worthwhile to request that after this law has received a fair trial of possibly one or two years the minister and his department keep an open mind on whether the fears of the police officers are justified. If police officers are being inhibited in their treatment of
Criminal Code
people they apprehend, some remedy should be sought in the future.
I wish to deal with the reason why police officers are concerned about the changes proposed in the bill we are now considering on third reading. I wish to quote from the 9th issue of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs. At page 15 I directed a question to Mr. Robert Brown, the associate vice-president of the Canadian Police Association. This man is from Toronto. I quote:
You seem to lay great stress on the danger of taking somebody who has been charged from the site of the arrest to a police station.
There are provisions that instead of the police officer trundling the accused to the police station, he may give him notice on the street that there will be court proceedings, and allow the man to continue on his way. I will give examples of this later. The police felt there was the danger of being open to some kind of civil action if they in fact took an accused to the station. I asked:
Do you think it would be an inhibiting factor on police officers?
Mr. Brown replied:
I think the way the bill is worded it would be because if that officer erred in judgment and found he had taken the wrong person to the police station, had taken a particular individual who should not have been taken to the police station, and that individual turned around and successfully sued him, there would be ramifications throughout all police departments across the country.
As a result of that and other evidence, changes were proposed which were satisfactory to the peace officers. They were in connection with what I call the power of non-arrest where someone is stopped and given notice that he is faced with a criminal charge but is not taken to the police station. Clause 436(2) of the reprinted and amended bill reads:
(2) A peace officer shall not arrest a person without warrant for
(a) an indictable offence mentioned in section 467_
I will deal with that in a moment. The clause continues:
. an offence for which the person may be prosecuted by indictment or for which he is punishable on summary conviction or	'

(d)	he has reasonable and probable grounds to believe that the public interest, having regard to all the circumstances including the need to
(i)	establish the identity of the person,

That is quite a mouthful. I would like to be hidden in the cloakroom of the police academy when someone is

speechtext:
On the discretion of the officer?
Mb. Turner: On the discretion of the officer. He has that discretion now, Mr. Chairman. This bill converts the discretion into a duty not to arrest and we are talking in this amendment as to what offences this duty not to arrest ought to be attached to.
Under the bill as it now stands the duty not to arrest includes all offences except for murder. Under the suggested amendment, the duty not to arrest would be restricted to summary offences, and there are about 100 of those, the offences for which there is an option to proceed by way of indictment or summary proceedings and those offences under the absolute jurisdiction of a magistrate.
Some of the police officers presented a good picture of the difference between the problems facing a police officer in a metropolitan area and those facing him in a rural area. I think the point was thoughtful and I should like to put some of the argument on record. The point comes from Mr. Brown, president of the Canadian Police Association of Toronto. He talked about the heavy onus which falls upon police officers in the street under the terms of sections 437 and 438.
We Intend to show, by exhibit, a number of items which could cause the officer on the street to accept certain identification as proof in dealing with a suspect. These identification documents. however, are either fraudulent or stolen. It is suggested that this is an urban police problem as opposed to rural.
Then they came in with a glittering array of documents, credit cards, student passes, train passes you name it-anything which anybody can open up their billfold and look at; all the cards they amass there. All these cards are the subject of forgery or fraudulent reproduction. The point Mr. Brown was making is that the police officer probably does not know the person he is stopping for crime in a big city, but likely would know him if he stopped him for crime in a small town. In a big city the one thing he would want, anyway, would be some identification of the accused before he would let him go under his own power; and Mr. Brown points out it is easy for a person of criminal bent to have all kinds of false documentation upon his person.
Well, time alone will tell whether this ready access to forged or otherwise fraudulent identification is an inhibiting factor for police. Perhaps there will be cases where public outrage will be raised because of the ability to obtain forged documents of identity and the like. But to me that is not really an inhibiting factor. I do not think it is a difficulty in the bill; I think it is just one of the reasons for our having a whole lot of police forces. Another point the same Mr. Brown makes is with regard to the principle of persons attending for identification purposes. Persons released may not appear to be the ones who attend an identification parade. This comes from the 9th issue of the deliberations of the Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
Different suggestions have been made regarding the mechanics of such a change in procedure. These have included obtaining a thumb print of the accused at the time of apprehension which would be the most definite form of future identification. We must consider the larger forces who process a number of prisoners each day. An officer may apprehend a female with short hair but when she arrives for identification she may be wearing a wig which would change her whole appearance. A police officer may

March 22, 1971

encounter some difficulty verifying the photograph as that of a woman he had previously apprehended, perhaps days before her identification appearance. The same could apply to a male with a beard and long hair who shows up clean-shaven and with a haircut. It would be almost impossible to identify the person from a photograph. We must also consider the number of persons a police officer contacts during his normal tour of duty.
I suppose that problem points up the tact that when in doubt the police officer will haul the fellow down to the jail for identification. That will be the big problem the minister will face because, let us face it, the minister is trying to cut down arrests and the arbitrary bundling off of people to put them behind bars for the night and let them argue for bail in the morning. In short, the minister is trying to achieve a more humane practice, but I suspect that unless you are stopped by your friendly, neighbourhood police officer who knows you, if you are arrested in a large city in Canada, 99.9 per cent of the time you will go to the jail and will have to argue your case before the desk sergeant.
I have two quick points to make before concluding. The first deals with guidelines for the detention of an accused in custody as laid down in new section 445A(7), which is to be found at page 24. I have already tried this one for size on some of my friends in the judiciary in Nova Scotia, and they found it vague. I do not know whether it can be any stronger than that which the minister and his drafters have brought before us, but for the record it deals with the detention of an accused in custody as justified on one of the two following grounds. In other words, it is an attempt to lay down guidelines for the direction of the judge or other persons who are dealing with bail.
(a) on the primary ground that his detention is necessary to assure his attendance in court in order to be dealt with according to law; and (b) on the secondary ground (the applicability of which shall be determined only in the event that and after it is determined that his detention is not justified on the primary ground referred to in paragraph (a)) that his detention is necessary in the public interest or for the protection or safety of the public, having regard to all the circumstances including any substantial likelihood that the accused will, if he is released from custody, commit a criminal offence involving serious harm or an intereference with the administration of justice.
That is, Mr. Speaker, if he is going to run out and try to "get at" Crown witnesses and suborn their testimony. But I think it does not express principles as quickly or efficaciously as Moses found when he brought those tablets back with him. The fact is that it does offer a primary and secondary line which judges should follow, and it may be worth while to look at again in a couple of years in light of the experience the minister finds the courts have in dealing with this problem. At least, to my mind it seems a reasonable direction.
Finally one is faced with the problem where a policeman has said; If you keep this man out of jail awaiting trial, he may go around committing other crimes. That is a pretty pertinent question, is it not? The Ouimet report, on which the bill is partly based, suggested having a registry in each province. In today's electronic age I am sure it would be possible to establish close liaison between the registries of each province so that police officers, judges or Crown attorneys could obtain very
Criminal Code
quick reports on subjects who had been apprehended and ascertain whether there was any likelihood of the person in question continuing to live a life of crime if given freedom.
Since I raised this point on second reading and it remained unanswered, may I just refer to Minutes of Proceedings No. 8 of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs, where as reported at page 30 I made the following remarks:
My first question relates to a suggestion within the Ouimet committee report that there be a registry system established within each province so that a judge faced with the question- a police officer, I presume, too-whether a person should be allowed at large or kept in custody to await trial would have some quick way of finding out about that person. This seemed to be a point on which Ouimet relied heavily but is, of course, absent from the bill. In fairness to that report perhaps the minister should be allowed to say why it is not in there.
The minister replied:
I agree with that suggestion of the Canadian Committee on Corrections, known as the Ouimet committee, but it is an administrative matter rather than a legislative one-and it is an administrative one depending on voluntary co-operation by the provinces. Under the Criminal Code the enforcement of the criminal law has been delegated to the provinces. It is their joint responsibility and I will undertake, as I already have undertaken to the hon. member, to transmit the Ouimet committee report recommendation to the effect that a central registry for bail applications be set up if at all possible. It might well be one of the matters that could be submitted to the uniformity conference next year, and I will undertake to do that.
I continued:
I suppose, Mr. Chairman, to carry the point further, there even could be co-operation, in this communications age, in respect of one central registry-
The minister replied:
Yes, and I imagine it will be done on the computer system now set up which handles a number of offences in a statistical way, automobile offences and so on, and the bail application problem could be put on the same system of computers.
I am sorry to have taken up the time of the House to make these three or four points on the bill, but I thought they should be on the public record, more especially since we had fairly good representation before the committee from those who will either make or break this bill. There is no doubt that it is the police officer on the beat who will prove either that we have been indulging in a great act of wisdom or in an act of optimism that has no basis whatever in reality. It would be my hope-I think I also express the hopes of my colleagues-that this legislation will do exactly what is hoped of it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on this bill. We had a healthy debate on second reading and a good discussion at the committee stage, so I shall confine myself to making just a few remarks. The test of the adequacy and strength of the bail reform bill will be shown when its measures are applied by an arresting officer, the officer in charge at a police station, magistrates, justices of the peace and provincial judges. The bill gives very wide discretion to an arresting officer, to an officer in charge and to justices of

March 22, 1971
Criminal Code
the peace. This will probably be a good thing because it will place on these people the onus of exercising good, common sense in regard to making arrests and permitting people to be released on bail.
In its present legislative form, the bill looks like a step forward. The principle that the financial means of a person who has been arrested and detained should not be the determining factor in deciding whether or not he should be released on bail pending trial is a step forward, as is the principle that the onus of establishing why bail should not be granted is on the authorities concerned. The test now in legislative form is whether an accused is likely to turn up for his trial. This test has been stated in many cases, and since we now have it in legislative form this is certainly another step forward.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that when the minister introduced the first bail reform bill in June he imposed on an arresting officer the duty of establishing reasonable grounds for justifying the arrest; no other grounds for arrest were adequate. The minister indicated at that time that any unjustifiable arrest might leave an arresting officer open to civil liability. Following conversations and discussions with police associations across the country, the minister made a substantial change in the bill which he later introduced. He has now set forth guidelines to assist a police officer who is making an arrest without warrant. These guidelines are to be found in section 436 (1) and (2). The police officer is also protected by the law, because the bill states that he shall be deemed to be acting lawfully and in the execution of his duty.
The fact that 90 per cent of all arrests are without warrant indicates the heavy duty imposed on an arresting officer in regard to offences under the Criminal Code. The law is now in the same position that it was in prior to the introduction of the bill-the onus will be on the person arrested to show the arrest was unlawful in order for him to succeed in a civil action. I am not being severely critical of the minister for his making that change. He has had the opportunity of speaking to police officers across the country, so we shall have to await the test of time to determine the adequacy and fairness of this provision.
I recall when we were in committee asking detective Syd Brown whether he had heard of any successful civil actions for unlawful arrest. If my memory serves me correctly, he said that in his 20 or 24 years' experience he had heard of no such successful action. There was certain apprehension on the part of the police in regard to the stringent sections in the Code prior to the second bill that was introduced by the minister. I think the minister will have to give some direction to arresting officers in regard to what they should do when making an arrest. The minister will probably have to set forth some of the charges in connection with which an arrest can be made, so the officer can issue the appearance notice at the time of arrest. I also think the minister will have to give similar indication to the officer in charge of a station before any issuance of a promise to appear on notice.
Time will indicate the effectiveness of these measures. We have given an arresting officer wide discretion, and I
expect that in the application of the new law there will be wide variations of application. We shall constantly have to scrutinize the behaviour of arresting officers in relation to charges brought under the Criminal Code.
I am very pleased the minister has included a clause in the bill which gives a magistrate the opportunity, when imposing a sentence, to take into account the time an accused person has spent in jail while awaiting trial. This has been very important in the past when sentence had to be passed. One situation which comes to mind concerns a second offence of driving while impaired. Under the Code, if a person was found guilty of a second offence of driving while impaired the magistrate had no discretion; he had to impose a jail sentence of 14 days minimum or a maximum of 3 months. If such a person did not have bail money it meant that he could spend upward of a month in jail and then would have to serve the mandatory 14 days jail term required by the Code. The provision which gives the magistrate an opportunity to take into account the time in jail spent by an accused while awaiting trial is a great step forward.
My last point is rather important. We have permitted an accused cash bail or other security in cases where he does not ordinarily reside more than 100 miles from the place where he is in custody, with the onus on Crown counsel to demonstrate that none of the other methods are satisfactory. I am sure the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) did some mental wrestling in respect of this particular provision and has come up with something which he believes adequate, reasonable and fair. I should like to remind the minister of the question I posed to him the other day concerning students, young people, who will be travelling across Canada during the summer. I can picture many of these young people perhaps getting into trouble with the municipal police and finding themselves in a position of being 100 miles away from their ordinary residence.
It may be that Crown counsel will try to demonstrate there is no satisfactory method of releasing such a person. We heard of cases last summer where a number of students were detained under the vagrancy sections of the Criminal Code. It seems to me we should not continue this practice of harassing young people and students who travel across the country. The only way out in this regard is for the Minister of Justice to rescind the vagrancy sections of the Criminal Code. This would take away from the municipal police the power of harassment in respect of students or young people who travel across Canada. Therefore, I again plead with the Minister of Justice, in my awkward but persuasive style, to bring forward an immediate amendment to the Criminal Code to delete the vagrancy sections and stop police harassment of students who travel across the country in the summer.
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning I said the test of this bill is dependent on the wise discretion exercised by the arresting officer at the scene of the arrest, or by the officer at the station, the justice of the peace, the magis-
[Mr. Gilbert.)
March 22, 1971

trate or the provincial judge in court. I should like to think the minister has taken a bold step forward with regard to protecting people from unlawful arrest and long detention while awaiting trial. I will probably have to wait at least a year to see whether I should throw accolades to the minister or continue the constructive criticism which from time to time I impose on him.
At this stage I am prepared to give the minister credit for this bill. I would say again that it is a mini-step forward with regard to our criminal law processes. I thought the minister took a big step forward in respect of the omnibus bill amendments to the Criminal Code. Now he has taken a mini-step. I should like to see him take another giant step by bringing forward another omnibus bill to take into consideration vagrancy, uniformity of sentencing and many other features with which I am sure he is anxious to proceed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to see the bill reach this stage. Reform of bail procedures is long overdue. Many anxious parents have wondered where a wandering boy has been, only to find some 24 hours later that he had become involved with the law. In many cases this has not been without cause, because sometimes young people have done something which, if not warranting arrest, warrants their being brought before a justice in order to give an account of themselves.
However, particularly in respect of a young person who has not done anything very serious, who has no record of previous brushes with the law and is a resident of the town concerned, it is particularly distressing for someone to have to go down to the jail and dig him out.
Criminal Code
It is always distressing. Also, when a young person is a long way from home and is trying to be independent, he does not like to have to phone home to mother the first time he has an extra bottle of beer or breaks an obscure section of the traffic act and finds himself arrested by an overzealous policeman.
I believe I know whereof I speak in this regard because at one time I was a green young policeman anxious for promotion. Sometimes the young green policeman who does not know his job is a little overzealous. He thinks it is easy for the young person to shrug off the fact that he has been arrested or detained. Such a situation is distressing to any well-meaning young person and certainly to all those who are near and dear to him and who have his best interests at heart. So I am glad to see this long overdue improvement made in respect of bail and the laws of arrest. I think, however, that an ounce of prevention-to be trite-is worth a pound of cure. I do not think that even with the law as it was there would have been very many arrests if all our police officers had been well trained in their duties.
Therefore I would appeal to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), because I know this subject is dear to his heart, to see that our police forces are adequately staffed. At present all municipalities are seeking money for low-cost housing, for anti-pollution, and for all sorts of improvements, and I think that the adequate staffing of police forces often takes low priority. I know the minister will use his best offices to encourage our municipalities, provinces and jurisdictions in which the federal government holds sway to ensure that police forces have the proper personnel. It is also very important to give our police forces proper training. I would like to see more facilities provided for our police colleges, not only to train young fellows on the beat but also to train higher ranks and to retrain some of the senior officers who set the tone of the whole police force.
On some occasions-rare, I hope-our police forces have been used as revenue men. Promotions are sometimes based on the number of prosecutions made. If this practice is allowed to go unchecked, a great barrier will be built up between the public and the police. Under no circumstances should we foster the belief that the police are anything but the servants of the public, in the highest sense. They are there for the protection of the public. The police, above all others, should be working to keep our young people out of trouble, rather than to lay traps for them or involve them in unecessary brushes with the law.
Until I read the bill carefully I thought there was a shift of onus which would put policemen on the spot and perhaps involve them in unecessary law suits. But as I read the legislation it seems that very little change is anticipated in this regard, and where a policeman has reasonable grounds for believing that an indictable offence has been committed, his powers will be very much as they were before, except for certain specific instances. He is given the same discretion if he acts in good faith,

March 22, 1971
Criminal Code
comes before the court at the correct time and explains the reasons for the arrest.
I never had any difficulty in this regard; 1 never arrested a member of the public without having reasonable grounds for doing so. Only too often the grounds are there. A well-meaning policeman, properly trained in the law, should have no difficulty whatsoever in establishing that he was acting in the best public interest, for the people and not against them. I do not think the onus which is put upon the accused or the person who thinks he has been subject to unlawful arrest is very great. Under section 436(3)(b) it appears that the onus is on the accused to establish a case against the policeman. But I think it is right that all he would have to do is allege that the policeman had in fact arrested him falsely, and I am sure that any justice worthy of the name would have the police officer come forward and explain why he thought it was in the best interests of the public to arrest the person.
I was also a little worried that this might be a technical act which would prevent the policeman doing his job while on extended duties, perhaps in the Arctic or in outlying districts where a justice of the peace was not available. However, I see that the onus is not necessarily on the policeman to bring the accused before a justice of the peace in the usual 24-hour period: the usual common sense of the Canadian public will prevail and he can bring the accused before the court within reasonable time. Here again, I do not think it would be difficult for the policeman to show the justice of the peace that it was necessary to bring the accused by dog-team from the Arctic Islands to the officer in charge in Aklavik, Coronation, or some such place where there was an effective or efficient justice of the peace.
So by and large I am pleased to see this long-awaited improvement to the Criminal Code in these two aspects. I have had considerable correspondence on this matter, perhaps because I have been a police officer. I will conclude after making one more request of the Minister of Justice, and that is that I think we are pitifully short of justices of the peace. I think that, particularly in cities, we should have justices of the peace on duty 24 hours a day so that in middle of the night persons arrested, particularly those from out of town, can come before a justice of the peace almost immediately.
With radio-equipped cars and the facilities we now have it should be a simple matter for a policeman to bring an accused before a justice of the peace and put the case before him briefly as to whether or not it is necessary to hold the man in custody. I think that particularly in our cities we should have justices of the peace on call so that these cases could be disposed of and so the onus of keeping the man in custody would not be upon the police. This would help to maintain the excellent relationship we have learned to expect between the police and the public. If the onus of keeping the accused in custody were taken off the police officer on the beat, he would then merely be a fact-finding man. In many cases the policeman is expected to use judicial discretion because the public thinks he is a fact-finder, judge, jury and court of appeal all in one.
