speechtext: The House resumed, from Thursday, January 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Goyer that Bill C-192, respecting young offenders and to repeal the Juvenile Delinquents Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs; and the amendment of Mr. Woolliams (page 2381).

subtopic: PROVISIONS REGARDING CHILDREN AND YOUNG PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a great many people across Canada are deeply concerned about this bill, the Young Offenders Act as it is called. Perhaps nothing could more effectively emphasize their concern or the need for modern legislation to deal with children and young people who have committed offences against society than the tragic case raised in this House last Friday by my colleague, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard). It was the case of a 14-year old boy sentenced to six years in penitentiary for the fatal beating last August of a 14-year old girl near Hope in the Fraser Valley. The boy was high on LSD at the time. It was all a terrible matter-but how was it handled? The judge, sending the boy off for six years to the penitentiary, said he hoped the boy would be sent to a minimum security institution. In other words, it was a case of out of sight, out of mind. What happens to that boy now? My colleague said he thought it was shocking that the boy should be sent to an institution which was nothing less than a school for crime.
The people of the country ask what will happen to this boy when he graduates from that school for crime? We have had a number of cases in my province-and I know there have been similar cases in other provinces-where young people, having been released from such institutions have committed even more dreadful crimes. This was because they had not been given the proper treatment or handled in a way that would guarantee their safe return to society. The case I have cited is an illustration of the failure of our method of dealing with young persons who have committed offences. It also points to the concern which people now have when they are faced with this new legislation.
Clause 4 of the bill reads:
This act shall be liberally construed to the end that where a young person is found under section 29 to have committed an offence, he will be dealt with as a misdirected and misguided young person requiring help, guidance, encouragement, treatment and supervision and to the end that the care, custody and

March 22, 1971

discipline of that young person will approximate as nearly as may be that which should be given by such a young person's parents.
But having given this lip service to the parenthood that was never extended to these delinquent young people, the bill forgets all about how successful parenthood works. In fact, it has been described by one official of the John Howard Society as a charter for young criminals. Any hope of providing the guidance and direction that such young people need, if they are to return safely to society, is doomed from the start. The bill starts out by paying lip service to the idea of rehabilitating young people, but then descends to a collection of legal terminology, spelling out the punishment that is to be given to a young person. The most damning criticism of the bill has come in a letter to members of Parliament and Senators from the Canadian Mental Health Association, in these words:
It is, in fact, a criminal code for children, which is distasteful in its terminology, legalistic in its approach and punitive in its effect.
In other words, the bill is clearly based on the old, outmoded concept of crime and punishment rather than on the new thinking of rehabilitation and redirection. Police techniques spelled out in the bill, such as fingerprinting, photographing and the establishment of criminal records that can only be removed under the criminal record act, surely have no place in legislation designed to approximate as nearly as may be the care, custody and discipline of young offenders by parents. If parents were to start out by fingerprinting, photographing and undertaking all these other legalistic things, very shortly they would have less, rather than more, influence over their children.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, we believe that the title of the bill is wrong. It refers to young offenders. We think this should read, as is the case in Britain, the Children and Young Persons Act, or simply the Young Persons Act. But that is the least of our concern. What is more seriously lacking in the bill is provision for an indeterminate sentence for children who have departed from the line of acceptable behaviour in society. How can a judge measure the exact amount of time required for treatment in the case of each individual? People's backgrounds, temperaments and requirements vary tremendously. I notice that Judge Little, chairman of the Ontario Juvenile Court Judges' Committee on Delinquency, commented:
They are assuming that a judge can measure the required amount of treatment. With a time limit, it's like taking a person out of hospital in the middle of treatment.
The Canadian Mental Health Association is even more explicit in this regard. It has stated:
A Criminal Code based on the notion that specific offences merit a specified range of punitive procedures may be appropriate for adults but definitely not for children. A particular offence may be committed by two children of the same age. In one case the total social, emotional and intellectual needs of one child may require only a suspended sentence; while the other child an indefinite and probably prolonged period of re-education, treatment and retraining may be required.
Young Offenders Act
The experience in my province, Mr. Speaker, is that an indeterminate sentence is much better than establishing a time limit, because it allows the people who are dealing with the child to determine, as the child progresses, much more exactly how much time is required. Young people change very greatly during the age range covered by this bill. That brings up another point, Mr. Speaker. We are unhappy about that age range. The bill covers the age from 10 to 17 years. We think that the United Kingdom approach, where 14 is specified as the minimum age, is better; and we believe that 18 years should be set as the upper limit. This is in line with the kind of treatment that is being given in Holland and Sweden, countries which are using a far more flexible method of dealing with young people than that laid out in the legalities of this bill.
What is also lacking in the bill is any provision for after-care and rehabilitation following release. It seems to me that there is not very much sense in holding a young person in custody for months or years and then throwing him back into the same circumstances which caused the commission of the offence in the first place. If this bill is designed to rehabilitate young people and restore them safely to society, provision must be made for after-care and rehabilitation. It is no wonder that Dr. Marcilio, until very recently head of the Toronto Family Court psychiatric unit, was moved to comment:
These children are not young offenders. They are victims of situations, of phychiatric situations and emotional deprivation. Eighty-five per cent of the children who come to the courts need psychiatric understanding, he says, but the proposed bill would disregard a child's need for help.
And Judge William T. Little, chairman of the Ontario Juvenile Court Judges' Committee on Delinquency was quite specific in his criticism of the bill when he said:
The intent of the original act (the Juvenile Delinquents Act) was to have a social objective of the rehabilitation of children. It seems to me this intent has been lost in the new bill.
But it does not come out as rehabilitation and redirection; it comes out into a crime and punishment deal all over again. The minister said that the new bill will treat young people as more responsible beings. Surely, like the rest of us, he ought to know that young delinquents are not responsible, and cannot be responsible, unless we are prepared to provide a whole range of resources to help them. They would not have committed unacceptable social behaviour if they had been responsible human beings. It is useless to expect that by the fact of arrest and committal they will suddenly become responsible human beings.
It seems to me that with this sort of approach we have not learned very much over the last few years. If a whole generation, and perhaps more, of young people is not to be lost under this bill I think we must bring its provisions into line with modern scientific knowledge and thought. I realize that satisfying society's feeling of outrage and guilt by punitive legislation against young offenders might be sufficient for some people: they might

March 22, 1971
Young Offenders Act
think that this should be the purpose of such legislation. But it is certainly no way to help the young people of today to find their road through this time of confusion and change.
I do not want to minimize the fact that these young people have committed acts which are socially unacceptable. We cannot shut our eyes to that. They have to be treated and rehabilitated, not only so that they come out as human beings able to stand on their own feet but come out safe enough that they can be turned loose in society. They have to come out as responsible human beings. I realize that there are no proper institutions in the provinces at the moment but I think the federal government would be doing what it should if it helped in the financing and staffing of such institutions in order to give young people a chance to become rehabilitated and rebuilt into good citizens.
The Canadian Mental Health Association has said:
In other words, legislation of this kind should be designed with the interests of this child as its primary concern rather than the seriousness of the offence.
Such legislation should be flexible. It should have in mind that these youngsters should not be forgotten by this legislation when it gets beyond clause 4 which reads:
This act shall be liberally construed to the end that where a young person is found under section 29 to have committed an offence, he will be dealt with as a misdirected and misguided young person requiring help, guidance, encouragement, treatment and supervision-
These are the ingredients which must go into any program which will help rehabilitate young people. Serious people who have been dealing with young offenders claim that these ingredients are not found in this new bill. In its recommendations, the Canadian Corrections Association stated as follows:
The decision on whether a child goes to an institution and when he is to leave should rest with the child welfare authorities. Whether a particular child requires placement in an institution, and in which institution, is such a technical decision that it should be made by the child welfare authorities, not by the court. When the court thinks a child cannot be dealt with to advantage on probation, he should make him a ward of the provincial director of child welfare, or appropriate official, who will then make the decision whether foster home placement will meet the requirements of the case or whether an institutional placement is necessary. If institutional placement is indicated, the director of child welfare should decide which institution will best fit the particular child.
Also, the decision as to when the child is ready to leave the institution can be made properly only by the child welfare officials who are in constant contact with his progress in the institution. The consent of the court for the child's removal should not be required.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, we are dealing with very flexible, changing and sensitive organisms when we are dealing with young people who have been bent and twisted, in many cases, by their home environment and the ignorance and neglect of the people who happen to be their parents. This happens all too frequently. If we are to use our best knowledge to try and help young people recover from the early twistings and distortions in their lives, we will have to be a great deal more flexible
in our approach and less legalistic than is the case in this legislation.
I should like to reiterate the recommendation made in opening this debate by my colleague from Broadview (Mr. Gilbert), that we should seriously consider giving this legislation a hoist. We should allow the committee to go across the country and talk with people who have had experience in these fields, rather than some lawyers in ivory towers here in Ottawa. Lawyers do not always inhabit ivory towers, but probably too many of them had a hand in drafting this legislation. We have seen that the Canadian Corrections Association, the Canadian Mental Health Association and people like Judge Little in juvenile and family courts across the country are against this legislation because they think it is stiff and punitive.
It is a pity to put ourselves into a legal strait jacket when dealing with flexible human beings in a time of great change. Let us hoist the legislation until such time as we can bring modern thinking and modern penal procedures to the shaping and training of these youngsters.

subtopic: PROVISIONS REGARDING CHILDREN AND YOUNG PERSONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-192 purports to improve the penal law affecting young people. I think it is trying to do too much too fast. It is like motherhood-we are all for it. We must be very careful when redefining the criminal law that is to affect young people below legal age, and I use the term "legal age" in anticipation of changes to the bill that will be made either immediately or when the bill goes back to committee.
We are trying to say in this bill that children not of legal age need not accept their full responsibilities in this field: they are not fully responsible in connection with other fields and activities. That does not mean that there is no evil-doing among young people. We make a big mistake if we think that with the stroke of a pen, by changing legalistic terms, we can rid ourselves of evil among human beings who are below legal age. We must be hard headed about this and say when something is wrong. Only by adopting a down to earth approach to these things when they come to our attention can we do something about them.
I trust that we have left the Dark Ages far behind. I hope it will not be necessary for me to speak tonight against the imposition of corporal punishment. I hope that has gone. I do not countenance it, nor do other progressive, well-educated, civilized men.

subtopic: PROVISIONS REGARDING CHILDREN AND YOUNG PERSONS
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: PROVISIONS REGARDING CHILDREN AND YOUNG PERSONS
speechtext:
The first speech I made in this House was on the subject of corporal punishment. I said 13 years ago- and I have had no reason to change my mind-that nobody, but nobody, has the right to inflict corporal punishment on any person unless it is done through love, meaning one's parents. No legally-constituted group or authority, whether composed of psychologists, prison

March 22, 1971

wardens or anybody else, has the right to punish me bodily. If we must err, let us err on the side of humanity because unless done with love, corporal punishment does no good whatever. I am in some doubt even about the value of corporal punishment by one's parents. Sometimes as a last resort when she has tried all other psychological means of persuasion, mother applies her hand to that portion of the body which the Lord provided for it. But in society there is no love and, therefore, we must rule out corporal punishment.
When we talk about correction we mean that we must discipline a person. Here, presumably, that means taking away some part or all of one's liberty. I do not understand how in that area this bill takes a forward step. No matter what you call it, under this bill you will take away young people of tender years, lock them up and keep them away from the various sources of love which they most need. Apparently, in this society everything that is worthwhile costs money. I suggest that we must be prepared to pay if we are to be helpful in this field. To begin with, I think we might devote a sum-I take this figure out of my hat-of $20 million, which is only $1 for every man, woman and child in Canada, and set the money aside for proper research and groundwork in this subject. It is no good setting up institutions, reforming our laws and bringing in well-meaning changes if we do not know exactly what we are doing.
I do not think all our psychologists, social workers, policemen, lawyers, judges and members of Parliament put together can come up with a plan which will eliminate juvenile delinquency or criminal actions among young people. On the other hand, we must take a positive step now; it is long overdue, because thousands of lives have been broken as the result of our neglect in this important field. There are not enough psychologists, sociologists and allied workers in this field, and as a result I suppose we shall be forced to segregate these young people in institutions from other, so-called normal children. We must have a plan in this field.
I think this bill is hasty. If I may use a lawyer's term, I think we are putting these young offenders, or these young people who have made mistakes, in double jeopardy. We say we will not make criminals out of them, but the logic of this bill seems to indicate that we will take away their liberty and put them in the custody of people who in many cases are not trained in this field and are not willing to give the attention, technical care and skill that these young people require. They need highly skilled care.
We are expressing a pious wish when we say these institutions will give the young people concerned the kind of care a child may expect from his parents. I presume we mean good parents when we say that. In the present complicated society in which we are trying to raise children in concrete tanks instead of natural surroundings, it is not easy to raise children who are happy and well adjusted. Yet presumably we will incarcerate these young people in institutions and leave them in the care of untrained persons who will not provide the kind of care that, in our pious hope, we wish for. They will
Young Offenders Act
not take the place of parents and it is patently impossible for them to do so at present. I say that we must act, even though it may now be too late, and spend money to train the necessary personnel. We must be very careful to make sure that the groundwork is done.
The bill suggests, Mr. Speaker, that we treat these young offenders as persons who will be locked up until they reach the age of 21, or legal age-which may be 18 by the time the act is amended. We are to keep them locked up until they reach legal age and then, in some cases, try them for their previous crimes as fully-grown criminals. The trial might be 11 years after the crime, misdemeanour or breach of society's rules: it does not matter what nice name one wants to call it. Ten or 11 years after the crime committed by the child, the fully-grown person will be tried. What kind of necromancy will take place in connection with a person who grows up in an institution, facing a trial for something which he committed half a generation ago? During those 10 or 11 years he is expected to grow like a well-watered flower in the greenhouse.
What kind of personality do you think a child will develop if for 11 years he lives under the shadow of delayed justice and does not know what will happen to him? If he is charged with a capital offence, he might be sentenced to another ten years in custody. Then you will find a person of 30 leaving jail and trying to adjust to society. It is not necessary to be a psychologist to know what kind of a twisted human being we will have in those circumstances.
I have had experience with the law. The best way to prevent a crime or misdemeanour is to convince a young person that there is a better way of life. He must be shown that if he does something wrong, justice will be swift: it may not be fierce, but it will be sure, fair and swift. He must be convinced that the sooner he starts back on the right road, the better. In a civilized society, rehabilitation is the only excuse for having anything to do with these people. They must be brought back into productive society as quickly as possible, with little emphasis on revenge and much emphasis on understanding and forgiveness. There should be no suggestion of a ten-year delay in getting at the root of the problem. A young person must be convinced that there is a proper place for him in society. He must be told that he is a person who counts, who will fit in and will come into contact with the love of the human race.
We must go out on the highways and into the hedges to locate those who like young people. We must not only attract them by high wages: we require well trained, dedicated people to take charge of young offenders. Even with such people it will be impossible to replace parents, family, race, religion and persuasion. These people must be given the same start in life which many of us had by the accident of birth.
This all boils down to the fact that we are leaving out one of the most important elements-the willingness of

March 22, 1971
Young Offenders Act
the Canadian people to pay. This cannot be done easily. What kind of institutions are they going to be put in? Are they going to be put in places like Bordeaux jail, well-meaning orphanages or industrial schools? The people who operate these institutions are no doubt wellmeaning, but it is shocking to know how often corporal punishment is administered. Corporal punishment which is administered, without love and understanding, to a child is completely wasted. The results inevitably bend the stick in the wrong direction. To beat a child you do not love will make him more hateful than before he committed the offence, midsdemeanour or whatever polite name it may be called when he does something of which we disapprove.
More social workers, psychologists and nurses must be trained. A great deal more than that is necessary. People are also required to look after recreation, including such things as teaching young offenders to play football. The people who staff our institutions are of a very high moral order. It is no exaggeration to say that a young male may be put in jail for three or four years for statutory rape. Statutory rape is committed when a boy of 16, for example, takes full responsibility for experimenting sexually. Where is the benefit of the doubt here? In Alberta, a boy of 16 can be jailed for contributing to juvenile delinquency because he had relations with a girl 24 hours short of her eighteenth birthday. Where is the benefit of the doubt there? If he is guilty of this offence, he may spend four or five of his difficult adolescent years in jail under homosexual guards-and certainly under the great threat of homosexual inmates.
The people looking after this young person should have the wisdom of Solomon and the integrity of a Roman mother. Where will we find such people? If we do not find such people, these young people will return to society after four or five years in such an institution so badly twisted that they will never become normal citizens. This will not be accomplished by this bill, the pious hope that we have done all we can for our young people because we no longer call them criminals. We are treating them like criminals; in fact, we are placing them in double jeopardy.
I do not suggest that the bill was not introduced with the best intentions. It has often been said that the road to hell is paved with good intentions. Are the good intentions to put young people into inadequate institutions, improperly staffed and subject them to the vagaries of sadistic guards or people who will use half-baked psychology upon them in an attempt to turn them into well adjusted, well trained, happy citizens? It is an impossibility! The members of organizations such as the John Howard Society and the Elizabeth Fry Society can do something significant. Their funds should be enormously implemented. These dedicated people are now working to the best of their ability in institutions in which people are called criminals. How much more would they be willing to extend their facilities if we put a little money into their care and trained more of the same kind of people to move in with these young people to make a home as closely as possibly to a normal home? I am not
necessarily speaking of people with university degrees, but people brought out of such societies as I have mentioned, the John Howard Society and the Elizabeth Fry Society, men and women with a degree of common sense.
The work they have already done in connection with paroles is wonderful, and I suggest that the emphasis should be on parole. The emphasis should be on getting these young people outside the prison walls as fast as we can and into surroundings as normal, happy and homelike as we can. The whole emphasis should be on de-institu-tionalizing the whole process.
As my experience has been for most of my life with delinquents, both of legal age and under legal age, I am not suggesting we should not hold hearings. I am not suggesting we should not bring to the attention of young people the fact that society is not happy with the way they sometimes behave. On the contrary, we need more staff, we need more and better trained policemen, more knowledgeable magistrates to see that these young people get a proper hearing.
Only a few months ago I was talking about bail and an improvement in the bail laws so that we do not confine young people unnecessarily in jail, not even for an hour, if there is any way of making sure that they are not deprived of their liberty and if they can be brought before a justice of the peace or a justice of the court and have their case explained on neutral ground. As a former police officer, I would have been delighted at any time to have shared the responsibility for an arrest and the judicial part of the judgment with a reasonable man in the community respected at all levels of society, a man who had no axe to grind, no promotion to expect, a man who in many cases had an intimate knowledge of young people. He should be such a person. He should be a person who knows the young people in the community, and he should be able to say, "In my opinion this young man need not be kept in custody." That is the kind of person we need on the bench. It is people of this kind who should screen our children of tender years, the most important natural resource we have, and it is with this original judgment that the whole future of this child and/or his family should be determined.
Improvements in the law will be an empty gesture unless we have enough people who make it their business to see that these young people are not damaged and that young people who have already been damaged are not further damaged by the well-meaning custody of people who are inadequately trained to look after them or help them once we have taken them out of circulation. It is ridiculous to try to set rules for treating ten-year old children in exactly the same way as you would treat a 17-year old. This act must be more flexible than it is in its present state.
Again I come back to the idea that we must have men of common sense and training to decide that a child must be treated as a child. When a boy is getting to be 16 or 17 years of age-when he should be, and certainly could

March 22, 1971

be, a man-he must not be treated as if he were a child of tender years. He must be shown that he owes it to himself and to society to accept some of the responsibility for his own rehabilitation. It would be ridiculous to take a boy of 16, in many cases fully capable of earning his own living, fully capable of fighting his way as a physical specimen through the world, and treat him as if he were a child just out of his mother's arms.
This bill should be divided into two parts so that we could get our thinking straight. One of those parts should be, if you like, a bill of rights for young people. We could put in it all the wishes, all the fine hopes for what we would do with young people. On the other hand, we should reform the criminal law in such a manner that a real effort would be made to set these young people on the road to recovery and to self-improvement. The only way of doing this is to completely forget any talk of punishment and revenue. The emphasis must be on providing an atmosphere which is closest to a happy home. An understanding of a child's needs should begin the day the authorities are aware that he has done something of which they disapprove. He must have competent help from social workers, psychologists, doctors and many people who do not fit into professional categories but who should be encouraged to give of their time and attention.

maintopic: CITIZENSHIP-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON CHARGES BY ALEX BANDY OF FALSEHOOD, DECEPTION AND INEFFICIENCY
CITIZENSHIP-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON CHARGES BY ALEX BANDY OF FALSEHOOD, DECEPTION AND INEFFICIENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago I asked the Minister without Portfolio in charge of citizenship if he would make a full report to the House in connection with charges of falsehood, deception and inefficiency levelled against the citizenship branch by a man in its employ, Alex Bandy of Vancouver.
The minister evaded a direct reply by indicating that the matter could be raised in the committee studying his estimates, and that as a member of this House I could discuss it there. I do not think this is good enough. The hiring and firing of Alex Bandy has raised a number of important questions involving government and public alike. Tonight I propose to ask some of these questions in the hope that this time the minister will realize the need for answers to be given in the House.
Why was Alex Bandy hired in the first place? As one of the leading figures at the poor people's conference from January 7-10, he was obviously acceptable to and trusted by low-income people on the west coast. Indeed,
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
he had been the secretary of the Unemployed Citizens Welfare Improvement Council in Vancouver for some time. The citizenship branch hired him on January 15, five days after the conference ended. Why did they hire him? According to Marian Bruce, in the Vancouver Sun of March 15, he believed his job was to discuss with low-income groups the possibility of government funding for community service projects initiated by the organizations. But in February, he said, he was ordered to start gathering information about the groups, how strong each organization was and what each group's make-up was in terms of age, ethnic background and militancy.
Meanwhile, from the moment of his appointment on January 15 he was under fire, first from British Columbia rehabilitation minister Philip Gaglardi and other Social Crediters in the B.C. legislature. They were joined by Liberal MPs from British Columbia, one of whom declared that the appointment of "aggressive demonstrators" like Bandy was unacceptable to British Columbia's 15 Liberal MPs. Apparently there was little or no consideration given to the fact that he was accepted by British Columbia's low-income groups.
Up to this point Alex Bandy had refrained from public comment, partly, he said, because Ottawa ordered him to remain silent. But the avalanche of political criticism, plus what he regarded as the political investigation he was ordered to conduct into low-income groups, proved too much. He spoke out vigorously, attacking the project on which he was employed as a "pacification project" designed to pacify and control poor people's organizations. He said the $44,000 spent on the project was a waste of taxpayers' money; that it could have been spent much better in direct funding to citizen groups. From the point of view of helping poor people, this money had been wasted, and so he was fired by the citizenship branch. I suppose technically his contract ran out.
A story by John Clarke, of British Columbia, in the Globe and Mail of March 20 says that according to federal officials Alex Bandy's project was part of an over-all scheme by Ottawa to help poor people's groups to develop a stronger voice in influencing national policies. It was meant to give the poor as much chance as business, labour and other groups to influence government programs. If this is so, why did the government crack down on Alex Bandy when he started to criticize the direction the project was taking, which according to him was not the direction it was taking when he was first employed? The government certainly knew that Alex Bandy was an outspoken person. Was that why they hired him-so that he could articulate what the poor people were thinking? Or did they hire him with the idea that they could silence him when his opinion differed from that of the government? Is the government now going to give up trying to help poor people organize themselves? Or will it look for more "Uncle Toms" to be grateful to be taken on staff-grateful and silenced?
These are all questions that need answering. I believe the minister owes it to the taxpayers, and the low-income

March 22, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion groups particularly, to give us a full account of the Alex Bandy affair.

speakeroldname: Mr. Barnett J. Danson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
maintopic: CITIZENSHIP-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON CHARGES BY ALEX BANDY OF FALSEHOOD, DECEPTION AND INEFFICIENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reply on behalf of the minister reads as follows. The federal government knew the risk it was running in appointing Alex Bandy to organize low-income groups outside the lower mainland. But to the federal government he had one thing going for him: he apparently could identify with the poor and the underprivileged. It obviously felt he could be a point of contact with the poor in its action, its research and stimulation of an employment project that was meant to help give them a voice in national policy development in the same way as business, labour and other groups. He has now thrown the job back in Ottawa's face with a confession that betrays the trust the government had placed in him and exposes a lack of understanding of the job. He says, "The idea of sending poor people out to research after poor people is giving some people a vested interest in poverty".
This is unworthy of a daring and imaginative proposal to get the picture of poverty from the inside, from those who suffer from it rather than from an army of social workers and statisticians. Surely, the government was saying, "We know about poverty from the outside; let's hear from the inside." To characterize it as a political subterfuge is misunderstanding the program's purpose and may deny the poor access to the one institution that can really help them, the government.

Mr. Speaker, on March 17, in reply to a question by the hon. member for Prince Edward-Hastings (Mr. Hees) the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) dealt with the appointment of a science ministry. As recorded at page 4347 of Hansard, the right hon. gentleman stated:
As soon as the House sees fit to pass the government reorganization bill we shall consider the appointment of a minister to deal with science matters.
I followed with a supplementary question in which I asked, in part, whether he would undertake to tell us, when the appropriate stage of the reorganization bill is reached in committee of the whole House, what other ministries of state, in addition to science, he proposes to set up in the near future. The Prime Minister replied:
Indication has already been given that we would wish to have a minister of state designated for the purpose of looking at housing and urban affairs. That is one other area.
He then mentioned environment, but environment is specifically mentioned in the organization bill. Then later he said:
-obviously I cannot foretell which areas might have to be covered by special ministers in the future. I have just mentioned two and it seems to me this clearly indicates the urgency attached to the passing of this bill by the House.
That is his argument. I thereupon looked back at the Throne Speech debate to see how the Throne Speech
(Mrs. Maclnnis.l
dealt with the ministries of state. I found these specific references:
To foster co-ordination of the activities of all levels of government, and to contribute to sound urban growth and development, the government proposes the reorganization of its urban activities under the direction of a minister of state for urban affairs and housing.
In the next paragraph there is this reference:
-the government will consider with care measures recommended by the Senate Committee on Science Policy and the Science Council of Canada.
Several paragraphs later we find this:
There will be proposed the establishment of a department to be concerned with the environment and the husbanding of those renewable resources that are part of and dependent upon it, with a mandate for the protection of the biosphere.
There, Mr. Speaker, are the references to the guts of the matter of reorganization. Perhaps it should be noted that the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Andras), who speaks for the government on housing, mentioned in the special one-day debate on the report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women that perhaps there would be a minister responsible for that as well. So we are probably being told by the government there will be a ministry of science, a ministry to deal with urban affairs and perhaps a ministry to deal with women. The Prime Minister suggests these can be established very quickly by the passage of his organization bill.
I am here tonight because I believe it must be made abundantly clear to the Prime Minister and his colleagues, if they do not know it now, that there are members on the opposition side and indeed on the government side who would like to make suggestions concerning what a minister of urban affairs should do; that there are members on all sides who would like to make known to the government what they believe any organization concerned with science matters should do; and that there are any number of members, if we are to have a minister responsible for the affairs and problems of the ladies of Canada, who I am sure would like to acquaint that person with their views concerning what his responsibilities should be and how they should be established.
So by laying out on Hansard the answer he did, the Prime Minister has in effect let a very large cat out of the bag. It is impossible now to take the organization bill and go through it quickly, because we know that when we come to the matter of the creation of these ministries of state we will have to put forward our views on urban affairs, on science policy and on the problems set out in the report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. That will be our only opportunity to do so. If we do not speak on the organization bill we will suddenly find ourselves presented by the Prime Minister and the government with a fait accompli and the people will ask where we dunces were and why we had no suggestions or ideas to present to the government in setting up these ministries.
e (10:10 p.m.)
So if the government did not realize what problem existed before with regard to its organization bill, let me
March 22, 1971

tell them that now they know and they had better get it divided first if they want some of the things like environment put into operation quickly, because I am afraid these other things will take a long, long time.

speakeroldname: Mr. Barnett J. Danson (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to answer my friend, the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave). Perhaps his closing words are the best reason for passing this bill as rapidly as possible, because it presents the dilemma of trying to speed up the work of this House to try to obtain the apparatus of government which will allow us to deal with very important matters. Yet we see some very small issues on which the business of the House can be tied up for a great length of time.
The ministry for housing and urban affairs has been mentioned and it is quite clear to everyone that it is a priority for this government, as is the ministry of science. As was mentioned by the Minister without Portfolio responsible for housing (Mr. Andras), the establishment of a ministry concerned with the status of women is another possibility.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
But the bill itself does give this flexibility to move. However, it raises the dilemma, which the hon. member mentioned, of how much debate we can stand and yet get along with the business of the House, with the things which we must do: what is the proper balance of debate that is essential to get the full expression of views from all sides of the House? It does give the government the flexibility to move without having to present a whole new reorganization bill each time it proves desirable for new ministries to be established. The concept of the ministries as policy-making groups, to avoid setting up a large bureaucracy and to have research and study in fields in which we are all concerned, is not in dispute. But it is impossible at this time to specify what additional ministries there might be if indeed they are ever filled.
The purpose is to give flexibility at that time. The three ministries which have been mentioned certainly have high priority for all of us in the House, particularly the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) and others who are concerned about these three very vital matters to our country.

maintopic: FINANCE-STUDENT LOANS-SUGGESTED CHANGE IN REPAYMENT REQUIRED
FINANCE-STUDENT LOANS-SUGGESTED CHANGE IN REPAYMENT REQUIRED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 8 I asked a question of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) regarding the repayment of student loans. My question was as follows:
In view of the present and expected high rate of student unemployment, will the minister consider making amendments to the student loan regulations so that students will not have to commence repayment of loans until six months after obtaining employment rather than six months after completion of studies, as is the case today?
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
In reply, the Minister of Finance said:
Mr. Speaker, this matter comes up for discussion each year between the provinces and ourselves. Of course, my hon. friend knows that where special circumstances exist the lending institutions can make provision whereby the repayment of a loan is deferred until the student is employed. Indeed, the repayment period can be extended up to ten years: the specified starting date can be varied by the lending institution.
Concern about this matter was first brought to my attention by one or two students who were concerned about finding employment upon graduation. As you know, today in Canada there are many students, not only those with B.A's but those who have Master's degrees and even Ph.D's who cannot And employment. Many of these students run up very large bills in student loans. This is also a concern of those who are not graduating from university, who for one reason or another have quit their studies. One of the reasons may have been lack of funds to finance their university education. In any case, Mr. Speaker, there is concern among many students about repayment of student loans.
Of course, all students want to repay these loans as soon as they can, but many of them cannot find jobs. If they cannot work out an arrangement with the bank or lending institution, they are in a real bind. The Minister of Finance said that special arrangements can be made with lending institutions. I would like to see provision for this written into the regulations, so that if a student cannot find a job he will not have to commence repayment of his loan.
Another matter which has been brought to my attention is that if a lending institution allows deferment of payment until the student has obtained employment, the student cannot obtain the same privilege that he had with regard to interest on the loan. If the government does consider amending the regulations, it should also take into consideration the matter of interest on student loans.
The reason this question comes to the fore today is that there is a great deal of unemployment in Canada. I do not want to get into a debate on that, except to say that possibly we have the highest unemployment rate in the industrial world. Some 8.1 per cent of our work force is unemployed. The government says this will be augmented by 1.8 million students, high school students, university students and post-graduate students this summer. When this happens, many students will have great difficulty finding employment. Even without taking students into account, the young people of Canada are bearing the brunt of the unemployment crisis because nearly half the unemployed are under the age of 25 years.
I would like the parliamentary secretary to give serious consideration tonight to this very small, piecemeal change or amendment to the student loans regulations, which would help students who will not be able to find jobs this summer and, more particularly, those who cannot find jobs upon completion of their university studies. I realize this would be only a very small step, but it would be better than nothing.
In the meantime, I hope the government will begin re-thinking its whole philosophy with respect to educa-

March 22, 1971
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion tion, because I do not think the financial background of a student's parents or of a student himself should be the determining factor in deciding whether or not he can continue his studies at the post-secondary educational level. I ask the parliamentary secretary to use his influence with the minister to amend the regulations and not leave it up to the financial institutions. I would also like him to persuade the minister that interest rates be considered when talking about deferred payment of loans. This would be one small step that would help many students as they fight to obtain university or post-secondary education.

speakeroldname: Mr. P. M. Mahoney (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
maintopic: FINANCE-STUDENT LOANS-SUGGESTED CHANGE IN REPAYMENT REQUIRED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the first place I should indicate that the government does not accept the forecast the hon. member has made regarding the consequences of students coming on the labour force, whether permanently or on a temporary basis, this year. There is certainly no admission or acknowledgement by the government that there are likely to be 1.8 million more unemployed people in Canada when the students come out of school this summer, as the hon. member would have us believe.
However, to deal specifically with the question he has asked, under the present legislation a student is not required to pay interest on a Canada student loan while he is a full-time student at an institution of learning that
offers courses at the post-secondary level and which is so designated by the province concerned. For a further period of six months after he ceases to be a full-time student, he is not required to pay any interest nor is he obligated to make any payments on the principal of the loan.
The regulations under the Canada Student Loans Act contemplate circumstances when a borrower may encounter temporary difficulties which will result in undue hardship if he must repay his loan under the terms originally agreed with the bank. Accordingly, provision is made for the bank, in consultation with the borrower, to revise any or all terms of repayment. I should emphasize that any revision is a matter for decision by the banks, subject to the overriding requirement of the act that any loan must be repaid in full within a maximum period of ten years. Repayment terms may, with the approval of the Minister of Finance, be revised to include for a period of time the payment of interest only and, in exceptional circumstances, for no payment at all.
